answer.answer:
Prefabrication/off-site work is the one enabler directly shown to drive improved site safety, since moving work off-site reduces on-site risk exposure. Beyond that single confirmed cause-and-effect link, several robotic-assembly-related enablers (robot arms, robotic pickup/selection, robotic assembly itself, human-robot interaction systems) tend to appear alongside site safety improvements in the same cases, but this is only a correlation, not proof that they cause safer sites. Site safety improvement is realized during the structural construction phase, so that is when to watch for it. If you want a defensible, evidence-backed safety strategy, prefabrication is the one to prioritize; the others are worth investigating further but shouldn't be assumed to be causal on their own.

Detailed answer:

The only directional dependency in the graph pointing to site safety is Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enables Improve site safety (VA13), because moving work offsite improves site safety. [1] This is backed by peer-reviewed evidence: peer-reviewed, Source: Li, Wang, Kassem, Alhajlah & Bimenyimana (2022), Evaluation method for quality risks of safety in prefabricated building construction using SEM-SDM, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 19(9):5180. [1]

No other enabler in the provided context has a dependsOn or enablesCapability edge targeting Improve site safety (VA13). Everything else connecting to site safety is co-occurrence data, meaning these enablers show up in the same cases as site safety improvements, but the graph does not establish that they cause it.

That said, the co-occurrence patterns are worth noting for practitioners investigating robotics-driven safety improvements, since they suggest where to look for further evidence:

- Robotic assembly (PR4) co-occurs with Improve site safety (VA13) at weight 13 [2], alongside robot arms, bespoke DFAB tools, DFAB contractors, and human-robot interaction.
- Robotic pickup/selection (PR15) co-occurs with Improve site safety (VA13) at weight 18 [3], one of its strongest co-occurrence links, also appearing with highly standardised processes and reliance on DFAB technology.
- Robot arm (RE2) co-occurs with Improve site safety (VA13) at weight 21 [4], alongside reduced human dependency and improved time efficiency, both plausible mechanisms for safety gains.
- Human-robot interaction (CO6) co-occurs with Improve site safety (VA13) at weight 28 [5], alongside improved human wellbeing and significant human involvement, suggesting collaborative robotics setups are frequently paired with safety gains in the same cases.
- Looking from the other direction, Improve site safety (VA13) itself co-occurs most strongly with Improve human wellbeing, Reduce time/efficiency, Supplier/manufacturer, Rely on DFAB technology, Significant human involvement, Reduce human dependency, Platform developer, Workforce training, DFAB Manager, DFAB engineer, Bespoke DFAB technology, and 3D Sensor/Camera/ICT [6], indicating that safety gains tend to cluster with broader digital fabrication maturity (sensing, dedicated management roles, training) rather than any single robotic technique.

Phase-wise, Improve site safety applies in the Structural Construction phase, with a phase span of Structural Construction and a value-realizing phase role. [7] So safety gains from prefabrication or robotics are expected to materialize specifically during structural construction, not earlier design or later finishing phases.

In summary: if the goal is a proven route to safer sites, prefabrication/off-site work (PR2) is the only enabler with a documented causal path in this graph. Robotic assembly, robotic pickup, robot arms, and human-robot interaction are all statistically associated with safety improvements across cases, and could be worth investigating as complementary or contributing factors, but treat them as correlational leads rather than established dependencies until case-specific evidence supports a direct link.
